# Ephemeris validation: Helios vs JPL DE421

**Status:** Phase 1, reference frames and large-body models. Generated by
`tools/ephemeris/validate.py`; every Helios number below was computed by the **C++ code**
(`helios_ephemeris_probe`, which builds a `helios::frames::FrameTree`), never by a Python port.

**Reference:** JPL DE421 (Folkner, Williams & Boggs 2009), 1900–2050, evaluated independently with
`jplephem`. Axes: J2000 ecliptic. Time: TDB seconds since J2000. Units: SI.

## Summary

| Model | What it is for | Result against DE421 |
|---|---|---|
| **Chebyshev** (`ChebyshevEphemeris`) | The real Solar System (stock universe) | ≤ **3 mm** for every body over 150 years (≈1e-15 relative: the float64 floor). Accelerations consistent with the true derivative to ≤ 7e-9 (the finite-difference floor). |
| **Frame tree** (`FrameTree::relative_state`) | Relative states between any two frames | Compositions through the lowest common ancestor add no error: Moon ← Earth 0.03 mm, Mars ← Earth 0.25 mm. |
| **Mean elements** (`KeplerianEphemeris`) | Procedural systems, fallback, planning | Inner planets **7–30″** RMS, Jupiter/Saturn **190–280″**, Uranus–Pluto **1.6–13″**, Moon **≈1°** (7,600 km). Comparable to JPL's published approximate elements (Standish). |

In short: the Chebyshev path is a faithful, numerically exact carrier of JPL's ephemeris,
which is itself accurate to roughly 0.2–0.3 km for Venus, Earth and Mars over recent decades
(the DE421 report's figure). The closed-form mean-element path behaves exactly as Keplerian
theory predicts, including its known failure modes.

## 2. Chebyshev model and frame composition

About 22,000 epochs: 20,000 uniformly random over 1900–2050 with random sub-second fractions,
plus up to 2,000 exact 4-day record boundaries of the lunar series, where discontinuities would show.
"Segment" rows compare one exported DE421 segment directly. "Composed" rows ask the frame
tree for a pair that is not stored anywhere, so the relative state has to be summed through
their lowest common ancestor.

![Chebyshev error per body](fig2_chebyshev_error.png)

| Target | Observer | Kind | Max Δr (mm) | RMS Δr (mm) | Max Δr / r | Max Δv (m/s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sun | SSB | segment | 0.00122 | 0.000167 | 9.3e-16 | 1.2e-14 |
| Mercury | SSB | segment | 0.0464 | 0.0109 | 6.7e-16 | 4.4e-11 |
| Venus | SSB | segment | 0.0682 | 0.0188 | 6.3e-16 | 2.9e-11 |
| Earth–Moon bary. | SSB | segment | 0.123 | 0.0311 | 8.3e-16 | 2.6e-11 |
| Earth | Earth–Moon bary. | segment | 0.0155 | 0.00732 | 3.5e-12 | 3.0e-12 |
| Moon | Earth–Moon bary. | segment | 0.0154 | 0.00732 | 4.3e-14 | 3.5e-12 |
| Mars | SSB | segment | 0.126 | 0.0391 | 5.9e-16 | 2.5e-11 |
| Jupiter bary. | SSB | segment | 0.49 | 0.131 | 6.4e-16 | 9.7e-12 |
| Saturn bary. | SSB | segment | 0.773 | 0.235 | 5.6e-16 | 6.0e-12 |
| Uranus bary. | SSB | segment | 1.54 | 0.459 | 5.4e-16 | 4.6e-12 |
| Neptune bary. | SSB | segment | 1.99 | 0.624 | 4.5e-16 | 3.6e-12 |
| Pluto bary. | SSB | segment | 2.99 | 0.819 | 6.4e-16 | 3.0e-12 |
| Moon | Earth | composed | 0.03 | 0.0103 | 7.9e-14 | 5.8e-12 |
| Earth | Sun | composed | 0.153 | 0.0343 | 1.0e-15 | 3.0e-11 |
| Moon | Sun | composed | 0.153 | 0.0342 | 1.0e-15 | 3.0e-11 |
| Mars | Earth | composed | 0.245 | 0.0556 | 2.7e-15 | 3.7e-11 |
| Mars | Sun | composed | 0.155 | 0.0418 | 7.4e-16 | 2.5e-11 |
| Jupiter bary. | Sun | composed | 0.622 | 0.142 | 8.0e-16 | 1.1e-11 |
| Jupiter bary. | Earth | composed | 0.503 | 0.144 | 7.5e-16 | 3.0e-11 |

The error grows with distance from the origin at a constant ~1e-15 relative level. That is
double-precision rounding, not a modelling error. The one exception to the 1e-15 level is Earth ← EMB (3e-12 relative):
the Earth sits only ~4,700 km from the Earth–Moon barycentre, so a 15 µm rounding error is
large *relative to that short vector*, but still only 15 µm.

### Accelerations (the frames' indirect term, BRIEFING §4.3)

The frame tree's acceleration is the analytic second derivative of the Chebyshev series.
It is compared with a central difference (±60 s) of JPL's own velocity:

| Pair | Typical \|a\| (m/s²) | Median relative diff. | Max relative diff. |
|---|---|---|---|
| Moon ← Earth | 0.0027 | 4.2e-09 | 6.7e-09 |
| Earth ← Sun | 0.00593 | 3.4e-11 | 7.9e-11 |
| Mars ← Sun | 0.00254 | 1.4e-11 | 4.6e-11 |
| Jupiter bary. ← Sun | 0.00022 | 7.3e-11 | 3.0e-10 |

The residual is the finite difference's own truncation error, ≈ (n·h)²/6. For the Moon,
n ≈ 2.7e-6 rad/s and h = 60 s, which gives 4e-9, exactly the level observed. So the analytic
acceleration is at least that good.

## 3. Mean-element (Keplerian + secular rates) model

Twelve parameters per body (six elements at J2000 plus six linear rates), fitted by least
squares on position to DE421 over 1900–2050 (`tools/ephemeris/fit_mean_elements.py`, output
`data/solar_system/mean_elements.csv`). Evaluated every 5 days over the whole window.

![Mean-element angular error per body](fig3_mean_elements_error.png)

| Body | Fitted around | RMS error (″) | Max (″) | RMS (km) | Max (km) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mercury | Sun | 7.0 | 27.5 | 1,903 | 6,138 |
| Venus | Sun | 10.9 | 27.5 | 6,187 | 14,436 |
| Earth–Moon bary. | Sun | 8.4 | 22.8 | 6,693 | 16,756 |
| Mars | Sun | 30.3 | 98.2 | 35,257 | 98,814 |
| Jupiter bary. | Sun | 188.3 | 473.1 | 765,687 | 1,698,968 |
| Saturn bary. | Sun | 278.6 | 555.4 | 2,182,392 | 3,924,057 |
| Uranus bary. | SSB | 13.1 | 65.9 | 220,343 | 882,707 |
| Neptune bary. | SSB | 3.1 | 11.3 | 102,266 | 298,170 |
| Pluto bary. | SSB | 1.6 | 4.0 | 64,885 | 163,816 |
| Moon | Earth | 3,719.8 | 8,597.0 | 7,563 | 15,169 |

How to read this:

* **Inner planets (7–30″).** A single Kepler ellipse per planet, with slowly drifting elements,
  already reaches arc-second level. The residual is the planets' mutual perturbations.
* **Jupiter and Saturn (190–280″).** Their 5:2 near-resonance, the "great inequality" with a
  period of about 900 years, cannot be represented by linear rates over 150 years. JPL's published
  approximate elements (Standish) show errors of the same order for these two planets. It needs
  periodic terms, or the Chebyshev model.
* **Uranus, Neptune, Pluto: fit them around the barycentre.** Fitted heliocentrically, they showed
  ~850,000 km errors. That is the Sun's own reflex motion around the Solar System barycentre,
  about one solar radius, driven by Jupiter and Saturn. The outer planets effectively orbit the
  barycentre, so fitting them there cuts the error 4–13× (Pluto 24″ → 1.6″). This is recorded as a
  data decision in the fitter.
* **Moon (≈1°).** Expected. The Sun perturbs the lunar orbit strongly: evection (1.27°,
  31.8 days), variation (0.66°, half a synodic month) and the annual equation. The residual is
  mostly along-track:

![Moon residual decomposition](fig4_moon_mean_elements.png)

RMS by component over 2024–2025: radial 3,374 km, along-track 6,773 km,
cross-track 704 km.

**Consequence for the design.** Real-universe bodies use the Chebyshev model. Mean elements are
for procedural systems, where no "truth" exists and the Keplerian orbit *is* the definition, and
as a cheap, unbounded fallback outside the Chebyshev coverage. A moon of a procedural planet
around a procedural star is exactly Keplerian by construction.

## 4. Unit tests backing these results

`ctest` runs 58 tests. The ones relevant here:
* Kepler equation residual < 1e-13 for e ∈ [0, 0.999] over the whole M range.
* Vis-viva, angular momentum and orbit orientation invariants; state ↔ elements round trip,
  including the circular and equatorial conventions.
* Keplerian acceleration = d(velocity)/dt; the orbit closes after 100 periods to < 1 m.
* Chebyshev series reproduces an analytic uniformly-accelerated motion, its velocity and its
  acceleration.
* Frame tree: composition, antisymmetry, error paths, and **precision far from the root**. A Moon
  400,000 km from Earth, 8 kpc from the galactic root, is exact through the lowest common
  ancestor, while the naive root-relative difference is off by more than 1 km.
* **DE421 golden test**: a 19 KB excerpt of the exported ephemeris (`test/data`) reproduces
  jplephem states for Moon ← Earth, Earth ← Sun and Mars ← Sun to < 1 mm and < 1e-9 m/s.

## Not validated yet

Rotating (body-fixed) frames, vessel propagation (Encke and the tree-code gravity of §5.2),
L-point dynamics and warp invariance are the next Phase 1 steps. They will get their own sections.

## Reproducing

```sh
python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r tools/ephemeris/requirements.txt
# de421.bsp: https://naif.jpl.nasa.gov/pub/naif/generic_kernels/spk/planets/de421.bsp
# (sha256 a20a7139da04cbc462454634918e9a9ca69127044e2cc9d4f9c16e238d2deedc)
cmake --preset debug && cmake --build --preset debug
cd tools/ephemeris
python export_de_chebyshev.py de421.bsp de421_1900_2050.hce        # ~15 MB, not committed
python fit_mean_elements.py  de421.bsp ../../data/solar_system/mean_elements.csv
python validate.py --probe ../../build/debug/tools/helios_ephemeris_probe --kernel de421.bsp \
    --hce de421_1900_2050.hce --elements ../../data/solar_system/mean_elements.csv \
    --work ../../build/validation --out ../../docs/validation/ephemeris
```

The development container that produced this report could not reach JPL's servers. The kernel
used was the byte-identical `de421.bsp` redistributed in the `skyfield-data` package on PyPI
(sha256 above).
